lever.sourceSummary: The existing full mechanism claim/guide includes pivot position, effort/load and a force–distance trade.
lever.attributionLimits: Original low-load classroom model, not a safe method for lifting a real heavy rock or applying formal moment calculations.
lever.question: Original case: a stiff bar rests on a stable low pivot, a small model load sits on one side and the adult provides a suitable force meter at the other side. Identify each part, explain a seesaw/bottle-opener purpose, predict then compare two pivot positions with the same load. Keep movement small and hands clear; adult checks range and stability.
lever.expectedEvidence: Name effort, load and pivot/fulcrum and explain each purpose. Trace the bar rocking about its pivot, rather than call every point a straight-line slider. Explain why a long effort arm can reduce the force needed but makes the effort end travel farther; use actual safe readings if measured, not an invented ideal result.
lever.nearMiss: Says the bar creates energy or extra lifting for free, every lever reduces effort or moving the pivot cannot matter.
lever.changedCase: Switch to a short-effort-arm lever such as a supplied tweezers example: explain that some arrangements trade a larger effort for a larger/faster or more controlled load movement, without claiming the old force benefit holds for every lever.

fixed-pulley.sourceSummary: The existing full claim/guide distinguishes a fixed wheel changing pull direction from movable-pulley effort reduction.
fixed-pulley.attributionLimits: Original small model; friction means actual readings need not equal ideal values. No suspended load over a person, body loop or real lifting use.
fixed-pulley.question: Original case: a fixed low classroom wheel turns on an axle; a cord runs over it, with a small flag model at one end and an accessible hand-pull at the other. Identify wheel, axle/support, cord, effort end and load, and explain how pulling one end down can raise the flag model.
fixed-pulley.expectedEvidence: Trace the hand/cord’s translational movement, the wheel’s rotation and the load’s upward movement as connected parts of one mechanism. Explain that this fixed wheel redirects the pull; it does not by itself halve the required force or create energy. Compare the actual directions from the specified positions.
fixed-pulley.nearMiss: Names only the whole device, cannot say what the wheel/cord/axle do, or attributes automatic force multiplication to every pulley.
fixed-pulley.changedCase: Move the fixed wheel to another safe support position: describe how the rope route changes while distinguishing that from adding a movable wheel.

movable-pulley.sourceSummary: The saved complete mechanism guide includes supporting cord sections reducing effort with a longer pull distance.
movable-pulley.attributionLimits: Original idealised explanation plus safe actual comparison where provided; no guarantee an unmeasured frictional model has an exact force ratio. The ideal comparison neglects the cord/wheel own weight as well as friction; actual records may differ.
movable-pulley.question: Original case: the load is attached to a low movable pulley supported by two cord sections. Compare its route with the fixed-wheel case using the same small load and adult-prepared safe apparatus; identify what moves with the load and where the hand supplies effort.
movable-pulley.expectedEvidence: Explain how supporting sections share the load and why reduced effort is accompanied by a longer hand/cord movement. Distinguish wheel position and function from the fixed-pulley case; keep force and movement descriptions linked.
movable-pulley.nearMiss: Says adding any wheel always reduces effort, or that a smaller effort lets the same energy appear from nothing.
movable-pulley.changedCase: The supplied model has higher friction than before: explain why actual force readings can differ from an ideal prediction while the basic support arrangement remains identifiable.

spur-gears.sourceSummary: Directly meshed external gears transmit rotary movement, turn oppositely from the same viewing side, and different sizes can trade speed for turning effect.
spur-gears.attributionLimits: Original external-gear case with compatible teeth and no slipping, not a universal rule for every internal gear, belt or chain. No ratio/torque equation demanded.
spur-gears.question: Original case: a small external driver gear turns a larger directly meshed external follower on parallel axles. Both are viewed from the same side and have visible position marks. Identify crank/driver, teeth, axles/support and follower, explain their jobs, and compare actual turns using an adult-approved slow hand-operated model or the supplied description.
spur-gears.expectedEvidence: Trace rotation through meshing teeth to the other axle; describe opposite rotation, with the larger follower turning more slowly and offering a larger turning effect for the same input, subject to losses. Distinguish turning effect from a claim that tooth-contact force magically grows. Link to a familiar geared hand mixer or clock purpose without operating a powered device.
spur-gears.nearMiss: Names gears but cannot identify input/output, says adjacent directly meshed external gears turn the same way from the same viewpoint, or says faster output and larger turning effect are both gained free.
spur-gears.changedCase: Insert a compatible idler between otherwise unchanged gears: explain how the final direction can change without changing the overall speed relation. Reverse which sized gear is driven and reconsider the speed/turning-effect relation.

plane-change.sourceSummary: The creator’s A5 text explicitly describes a spur/crown arrangement changing rotary orientation through a right angle.
plane-change.attributionLimits: Original orientation description of a valid right-angle arrangement, not an inspected copy of the source photo. No claim that all gears or all bevel/crown arrangements have the same angle/speed.
plane-change.geometryBefore: In this original supplied case, the input gear rotates in a vertical plane around a horizontal axle.
plane-change.geometryAfter: A correctly meshing crown/follower rotates in a horizontal plane around a vertical axle; the axes are perpendicular, so the plane of rotation changes.
plane-change.question: Original case: identify the driver, follower, meshing teeth, axles and support in a supplied slow right-angle spur/crown model or the explicit geometry description above. Trace the input turning movement to the output and describe the changed plane. Contrast with the parallel-axle spur case.
plane-change.expectedEvidence: Explain that both motions remain rotary but their orientation changes; the output turns in a different plane rather than simply turning faster in the same plane. Name which parts carry the movement and their purpose. Distinguish a plane/orientation change from reversal seen on two coplanar gears. A correctly prepared larger follower may also turn more slowly; do not infer an exact numerical ratio without its actual tooth counts.
plane-change.nearMiss: Calls every reversal a plane change or says any two gears must have parallel axles.
plane-change.changedCase: Rotate the whole model on the table: explain that page-up/page-right labels can change while the perpendicular relation between input and output axes remains. State viewpoints before describing clockwise/anticlockwise.

wholeClaimReview.cardAndGuide: Complete authored card, pedagogy, all4 learn activities, constraints, reviewNotes, assessment, sources and provenance read.
wholeClaimReview.reuseReason: Full existing guide already includes the part/purpose, movement transfer, speed/direction and force–distance relations. The supplied right-angle case applies that mechanism-transfer knowledge in another orientation; it does not establish a new generic motion-plane mastery node. Actual source-specific performance is assessed directly, not inferred from a previous mechanism score.
wholeClaimReview.limits: Whole force-effect reasoning and actual measurement requirements remain intact and separately checked. The later moments/pressure/Hooke bundle is not lowered; no new edges, inventory or quantitative prerequisite is introduced. No source figure/video was viewed or copied.
wholeClaimReview.hardClosureReadScope: All6 direct/transitive-hard cards and7 hard edges read; complete Q2 guide read. Existing balanced-force investigation/diagram, friction and vocabulary requirements remain readiness, not inferred mastery from these motion cases.

safety: All real models are adult-prepared, intact, slow hand-operated, low-load and used under school procedures. Keep fingers clear of mesh/pinch points, use large suitable parts, no body loops or suspended loads above people and stop before damage. Textual/model explanation does not become a claim the learner built or tested a mechanism.
